metadata.title: Non-Penicillin Beta-Lactam Drugs: A CGMP Framework for Preventing Cross-Contamination: Draft Guidance for Industry

candidates.statement: Penicillin can be a sensitizing agent that triggers hypersensitivity or an allergic reaction in some 32 people. 6 Drug cross-contamination is the contamination of one drug with one or more different 33 drugs or compounds. Accordingly, facilities and controls must be designed to prevent cross- 34 contamination of other drugs with penicillin in accordance with the current good manufacturing 35 practice (CGMP) regulations (i.e., 21 CFR 211.42(d), 21 CFR 211.46(d), and 21 CFR 211.176). 36 Because non-penicillin beta-lactam antibacterial drugs and non-antibacterial beta-lactam 37 compounds can also be sensitizing agents, drug cross-contamination with such compounds could 38 initiate the same types of drug-induced life-threatening allergic reactions that penicillins can 39 trigger. Therefore, manufacturers handling any non-penicillin beta-lactam antibacterial drugs or 40 non-antibacterial beta-lactam compounds should treat such drugs or compounds similarly to 41 penicillin to prevent cross-contamination, thereby reducing the potential for drug-induced, life- 42 threatening allergic reactions. 43
candidates.context: 5 See the definition of complete and comprehensive separation in the Glossary. The information in this guidance is intended for human drug manufacturers (including finished 45 pharmaceutical manufacturers, active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) manufacturers, re- 46 packagers, and outsourcing facilities 7 ) with operations that include one or more beta-lactam 47 compounds. 48

candidates.statement: 7 Section 503B of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act describes the conditions that must be satisfied for drug products compounded by a registered outsourcing facility to be exempt from certain statutory requirements. For the purposes of this guidance and for outsourcing facilities only, processing of beta-lactam compounds does not refer to mixing, reconstituting, or other such acts performed in accordance with directions contained in the manufacturer’s approved labeling and other manufacturer directions consistent with that labeling at the immediate point of dispensing for administration to the intended patient if these limited activities are performed via closed fluid- pathway, single-use sterile transfer devices under appropriate local containment controls to prevent facility exposure to beta-lactam compounds. Although use of these sterile transfer devices (accomplishing transfers through the use of needles and needleless connectors) greatly mitigates risk of lost containment while preparing a drug in accordance with labeled directions, it is possible that breakage or spillage of the content of a pharmacy bulk package occurs. To prevent the risk of facility (e.g., surfaces, air) and product contamination with beta-lactam compounds, the outsourcing facility should have in place additional containment strategies, including restricting all preparation activities to only dedicated isolators, barrier units, or containment hoods to strictly localize any potential exposure.
candidates.context: 6 The term sensitizing (allergenic) is commonly used in guidances for industry in discussions related to immunology. Use of appropriate procedures is also essential, including employing detailed steps for managing any localized aerosolization from a breakage/spillage incident by immediate and thorough decontamination with beta-lactam inactivating cleaning agent(s). The containment and decontamination procedures should be validated for their intended purposes of strictly preventing cross-contamination with beta-lactam compounds.

candidates.statement: Several CGMP requirements for finished pharmaceuticals address facility and equipment design, 88 controls, and cleaning. For example, regarding design and construction features, § 211.42(c) 89 requires building and facility provisions in general to prevent cross-contamination of drug 90 products. Specifically, the regulation states that “[t]here shall be separate or defined areas or 91 such other control systems for the firm’s operations as are necessary to prevent contamination or 92 mixups . . . .” 93
candidates.context: 21 CFR parts 210 and 211. 86 With respect to penicillin, § 211.42(d) requires that “[o]perations relating to the manufacture, 95 processing, and packing of penicillin shall be performed in facilities separate from those used for 96 other drug products for human use.” 8

candidates.statement: 12 After reviewing relevant scientific and medical literature, FDA determined that the relative risk of cross-reactivity associated with aztreonam, when compared to other beta-lactams, is a matter of scientific uncertainty. Recently there is an increased body of evidence in published scientific literature describing that patients with ceftazadine hypersensitivity can experience cross-reactivity to aztreonam. Accordingly, this guidance does not recommend manufacturing controls that treat aztreonam differently from other beta-lactam drugs. As with any nonbinding recommendations offered in guidance to industry, manufacturers can use an alternative approach if the alternative approach satisfies the requirements of the applicable statutes and regulations. Manufacturers should discuss with FDA as early as possible about alternative separation designs and control strategies for a non-penicillin beta-lactam monobactam, such as aztreonam.

candidates.statement: As discussed above, compounds containing a beta-lactam ring have a sensitizing potential, and 226 subsequent exposure to those compounds or related compounds due to cross-contamination may 227 result in severe allergic reactions in some patients. Therefore, manufacturers should manage the 228 risk of cross-contamination throughout the products’ life cycles, not only non-penicillin beta- 229 lactam antibacterial drugs, but also products with no antibacterial activity that may be potential 230 sources of a beta-lactam ring (e.g., degradants that contain a beta-lactam ring even though the 231 parent compound may not). 232

candidates.statement: Because of the potential health risks of cross-reactivity and hypersensitivity reactions associated 237 with beta-lactam compounds, manufacturers’ risk management strategies should include 238 stringent controls to prevent cross-contamination. 239
candidates.context: The risks associated with the cross-reactivity of beta-lactam antibacterial drugs have been 241 described (Terico and Gallagher 2014; Joint Task Force on Practice Parameters 2010; Çelik et al. 242 2008); however, the risks associated with the cross-reactivity of non-antibacterial beta-lactam 243 compounds are less well understood. Accordingly, FDA addresses beta-lactam antibacterial 244 drugs and non-penicillin beta-lactam compounds separately in this guidance. Specific 245 recommendations for beta-lactam antibacterial drugs and non-antibacterial beta-lactam 246 compounds are further detailed below. 247

candidates.statement: The manufacturing operations of any class of non-penicillin beta-lactam antibacterial drugs 251 should be completely and comprehensively separated from areas in which any other drugs for 252 human use are manufactured, including any other class of beta-lactam antibiotics. This 253 separation includes independent air handling systems. Manufacturing operations that are 254 restricted solely to products within a specific class of non-penicillin beta-lactam antibacterial 255 drugs (e.g., cephalosporins) generally would not mandate separate facilities and air handling 256 systems for each of those products; production campaigning in the same facility and appropriate 257 cleaning (including qualification to demonstrate removal of beta-lactams) after each campaign 258 may be sufficient to prevent cross-contamination. 259
candidates.context: A. Non-Penicillin Beta-Lactam Antibacterial Drugs 249 B. Non-Antibacterial Beta-Lactam Compounds 261

Thus, when there is uncertainty regarding the 270 risks associated with non-antibacterial beta-lactam compounds, or there is a known risk of 271 adverse effect in patients, FDA recommends that drug manufacturers implement a complete and 272 comprehensive separation cross-contamination prevention strategy, as is recommended for non- 273 penicillin beta-lactam antibacterial drugs, to prevent beta-lactam cross-contamination. 274
candidates.context: As with non-penicillin beta-lactam antibacterial drugs, non-antibacterial beta-lactam compounds 263 have the potential to induce allergic reactions. Similar difficulties exist in characterizing and 264 quantifying the potential health risks posed by non-antibacterial beta-lactam compounds (i.e., 265 defining the minimal dose below which allergic responses are unlikely to occur in humans, lack 266 of suitable animal or receptor testing models predictive of human sensitivity, and the likelihood 267 that the threshold dose for human allergenic response could be extremely low and difficult to 268 However, there may be conditions under which manufacturers may justify the use of alternative 276 cross-contamination prevention strategies for certain non-antibacterial beta-lactam compounds. 13

candidates.statement: For example, non-antibacterial beta-lactam compounds can have widely varying molecular 278 structures, and there may be cases where direct studies have shown no incidence of, or 279 exceedingly low potential for, adverse events involving hypersensitivity or allergic reactions in 280 patients. In such cases, if a manufacturer considers a prevention strategy other than complete 281 and comprehensive separation to suffice, robust data to support no incidence or a clear threshold 282 below which adverse reactions are exceedingly unlikely to occur should be available for FDA 283 assessment. An extensive body of data to evaluate this potential approach can include in vitro 284 data, animal studies, clinical studies, 14 experience with related products, and published scientific 285 literature. Manufacturers should use appropriate risk management tools to assess the risks and to 286 design and implement prevention strategies that prevent cross-contamination and mix-ups. This 287 would include consideration of a combination of rigorous facility design, segregation, process, 288 and procedural controls, and ongoing life cycle risk review. 15 Examples of such design and 289 controls provisions are provided in Appendix B. 290

candidates.statement: In other words, although separate buildings would ensure separation of beta-lactam operations 324 from non-beta-lactam operations, it is feasible for one building to contain a dedicated area for 325 beta-lactam manufacturing that is completely isolated and sealed off from the rest of the 326 building. For example, separate entries and exits to the beta-lactam segment of the building 327 would be necessary to ensure comprehensive separation. In the limited cases in which this 328 design concept could be considered, a risk assessment should demonstrate that the design 329 provides as much protection against cross-contamination as is achieved by manufacturing in a 330 separate building. 331
